The **Pretenders** are an English rock band formed in March 1978. The original band consisted of founder and main songwriter Chrissie Hynde (lead vocals, rhythm guitar), [James Honeyman-Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Honeyman-Scott "James Honeyman-Scott") (lead guitar, backing vocals, keyboards), [Pete Farndon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Farndon "Pete Farndon") (bass guitar, backing vocals), and [Martin Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Chambers "Martin Chambers") (drums, backing vocals, percussion). Following the deaths of Honeyman-Scott in 1982 and Farndon in 1983, the band experienced numerous personnel changes; American-born Hynde has been the band's only continuous member.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-2)

The band's hit songs include "[Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_(Pretenders_song) "Kid (Pretenders song)")" (1979), "[Brass in Pocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brass_in_Pocket "Brass in Pocket")" (1979), "[Talk of the Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk_of_the_Town_(Pretenders_song) "Talk of the Town (Pretenders song)")" (1980), "[I Go to Sleep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Go_to_Sleep "I Go to Sleep")" (1981), "[Back on the Chain Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_on_the_Chain_Gang "Back on the Chain Gang")" (1982), "[Don't Get Me Wrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Get_Me_Wrong "Don't Get Me Wrong")" (1986), and "[I'll Stand by You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll_Stand_by_You "I'll Stand by You")" (1994). The Pretenders were inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in 2005.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]

Hynde, originally from [Akron, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron,_Ohio "Akron, Ohio"), moved to London in 1973, working at the weekly music paper _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3) and at [Malcolm McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_McLaren "Malcolm McLaren") and [Vivienne Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood")'s clothes store. She was involved with early versions of the [Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols"), [the Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clash "The Clash"), and [the Damned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Damned_(band) "The Damned (band)") and played in short-lived bands such as [Masters of the Backside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_of_the_Backside "Masters of the Backside") (1976) and [the Moors Murderers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Moors_Murderers_(band) "The Moors Murderers (band)") (1978 lineup), but failed to find a regular or equal partnership in the bands she joined.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-4)

Hynde's own provocative band project, centred around her own songwriting, was initially called (Mike Hunt's) Dishonorable Discharge and featured former [London SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_SS "London SS") and future Damned members, along with [Mick Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Jones_(The_Clash_guitarist) "Mick Jones (The Clash guitarist)") and [Sid Vicious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sid_Vicious "Sid Vicious") (where Hynde taught Vicious to play guitar), but failed to get managerial backing from either Malcolm McLaren or [Bernie Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Rhodes "Bernie Rhodes"), despite them both poaching her band members for, or asking her to fill in, in their pet projects.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-6)

The Pretenders formed in 1978 after Dave Hill at [Anchor Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor_Records "Anchor Records") heard some [demonstration tapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demo_(music) "Demo (music)") of Hynde's music. He arranged a rehearsal studio in [Denmark Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_Street "Denmark Street"), London, where a three-piece band consisting of Hynde, Mal Hart on bass (he had played with Hynde and [Steve Strange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Strange "Steve Strange") in the Moors Murderers), and [Phil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_%22Philthy_Animal%22_Taylor "Phil \"Philthy Animal\" Taylor")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-7) of [Motörhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mot%C3%B6rhead "Motörhead") on drums played a selection of Hynde's original songs. Hill was impressed and arranged a day at Studio 51 to record another demo. Although it was rough, he felt he had seen and heard enough "star potential" to suggest that Hynde form a more permanent band to record for his new label, Real Records.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

Hynde then formed a band composed of [Pete Farndon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Farndon "Pete Farndon") on bass, James Honeyman-Scott on guitar, and Gerry Mcilduff on drums. This band, then without a name, recorded five tracks at Regents Park Studio in July 1978, including a cover of [the Kinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kinks "The Kinks")' song "[Stop Your Sobbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop_Your_Sobbing "Stop Your Sobbing")". Shortly thereafter, Gerry Mcilduff was replaced on drums by [Martin Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Chambers "Martin Chambers") (of [the Vacants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vacants?action=edit&redlink=1 "The Vacants (page does not exist)")).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-8) Hynde named the band the Pretenders after [the Platters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Platters "The Platters") song "[The Great Pretender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Pretender "The Great Pretender")",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-9) which was the favourite song of one of her former boyfriends.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-10)

### Original band (1978–1982)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Original band (1978–1982)")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/The_Pretenders_%281979_Sire_publicity_photo%29_01.jpg/250px-The_Pretenders_%281979_Sire_publicity_photo%29_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Pretenders_(1979_Sire_publicity_photo)_01.jpg)

The Pretenders in a 1979 publicity photo

The band's first single, a cover of the Kinks' "Stop Your Sobbing" (produced by [Nick Lowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Lowe "Nick Lowe") and recorded at the July Regents Park sessions) was released in February 1979 and gained critical attention.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3) It was followed by "[Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_(Pretenders_song) "Kid (Pretenders song)")" in June 1979. In January 1980, the band reached number 1 in the UK with "[Brass in Pocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brass_in_Pocket "Brass in Pocket")", which was also successful in the US, reaching number 14 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

Their [self-titled debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretenders_(album) "Pretenders (album)") was released in January 1980 and was a success in the UK and the United States both critically and commercially.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3) Produced by [Chris Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Thomas_(record_producer) "Chris Thomas (record producer)"), it is regarded as one of the best debut albums of all time,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-11) and has been named one of the best albums of all time by [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1") (number 52)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-12) and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ (number 155).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-13)

Their second full-length album, _[Pretenders II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretenders\_II "Pretenders II")_, was released during August 1981. It included the songs from the US EP _[Extended Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended\_Play\_(Pretenders\_EP) "Extended Play (Pretenders EP)")_, the [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV") video success "Day After Day", and popular [album-radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_oriented_rock "Album oriented rock") tracks "The Adultress", "Birds of Paradise", "Bad Boys Get Spanked", and "The English Roses".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Pretenders_Dec_81.JPG/250px-Pretenders_Dec_81.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pretenders_Dec_81.JPG)

The Pretenders (original line-up), Dominion Theatre, London, December 1981

On 18 September 1981, the Pretenders were the musical guest on the US late-night sketch comedy show [_Fridays_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fridays_(TV_series) "Fridays (TV series)"). The band performed "The Adultress", "[Message of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message_of_Love "Message of Love")", and "Louie, Louie" (not [the Kingsmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kingsmen "The Kingsmen") song). [Andy Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Kaufman "Andy Kaufman") was the guest host of the program on that night.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-14)

Due to Farndon's escalating drug abuse, he was fired from the band after a meeting between Hynde, Honeyman-Scott, and Chambers on 14 June 1982. Two days later, Honeyman-Scott died of heart failure as a result of cocaine intolerance. While in the midst of forming a new band, Farndon was found dead by his wife on 14 April 1983. After taking heroin and passing out, he had drowned in his bathtub.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

### Re-grouping (1982–1989)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Re-grouping (1982–1989)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/The_Pretenders_Learning_To_Crawl_%281984_Sire_publicity_photo%29.jpg/250px-The_Pretenders_Learning_To_Crawl_%281984_Sire_publicity_photo%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Pretenders_Learning_To_Crawl_(1984_Sire_publicity_photo).jpg)

The Pretenders in a 1984 publicity photo: An alternate photo from the same shoot would be used as the cover for _[Learning to Crawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learning\_to\_Crawl "Learning to Crawl")_.

Hynde and Chambers continued the band after Honeyman-Scott's death. During July 1982, a caretaker team of Hynde, Chambers, guitarists [Billy Bremner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Bremner_(musician) "Billy Bremner (musician)") of [Rockpile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockpile "Rockpile") and [Robbie McIntosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbie_McIntosh "Robbie McIntosh"), and [Big Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Country "Big Country") bassist [Tony Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Butler_(musician) "Tony Butler (musician)") was assembled to record the single "[Back on the Chain Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_on_the_Chain_Gang "Back on the Chain Gang")".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-15)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3) The song was released in October and became their biggest success in the US, staying at number 5 for three consecutive weeks. The single's B-side, "[My City Was Gone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_City_Was_Gone "My City Was Gone")" was (except for a few weeks in July and August of 1999) the theme music for _[the Rush Limbaugh Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rush\_Limbaugh\_Show "The Rush Limbaugh Show")_ since its inception.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-Limbaugh-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-mydad-17)

Hynde then set up a more permanent lineup for the band during the 1982 holiday season, keeping Chambers and McIntosh and adding [Malcolm Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Foster "Malcolm Foster") on bass. "Middle of the Road" was this line-up's first single, released in the US in November 1983 and reaching the top 20 there. The US B-side, "[2000 Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Miles "2000 Miles")", was released as a single in the UK. The third Pretenders album, _[Learning to Crawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learning\_to\_Crawl "Learning to Crawl")_ was produced by "fifth Pretender" Chris Thomas and released in January 1984.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

In July 1985, the band (including Rupert Black on keyboards) played at [Live Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_Aid "Live Aid").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3) Soon after recording sessions for the next album began and one track had been completed, Hynde declared that Chambers was no longer playing well and dismissed him. Discouraged at the loss of his bandmate, Foster quit ("My whole argument was that Martin Chambers was the rhythm section of the Pretenders and it didn't really matter who was playing bass. So I just said I didn't want to be involved any more."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-fosterguitarist-18)) Hynde and McIntosh recorded the rest of the album in various sessions in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") with assorted session musicians. Towards the end of the sessions, Hynde hired two of the guest players–bassist [T.M. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T.M._Stevens "T.M. Stevens") and ex-[Haircut One Hundred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haircut_One_Hundred "Haircut One Hundred") drummer [Blair Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blair_Cunningham "Blair Cunningham")—as the new Pretenders rhythm section. The _[Get Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Get\_Close "Get Close")_ album was released in 1986; the disc included the top 10 singles, "[Don't Get Me Wrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Get_Me_Wrong "Don't Get Me Wrong")" from the film _[Gung Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gung\_Ho\_(film) "Gung Ho (film)")_ (helped by a popular video homage to the television series _[the Avengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Avengers\_(TV\_series) "The Avengers (TV series)")_) and "[Hymn to Her](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn_to_Her "Hymn to Her")", a No.8 success in the UK.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3) In the US, both "Don't Get Me Wrong" and "[My Baby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Baby_(Pretenders_song) "My Baby (Pretenders song)")" reached No. 1 on the _Billboard_[Mainstream Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_Rock_(chart) "Mainstream Rock (chart)") chart.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-19)

For the _Get Close_ tour, [Bernie Worrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Worrell "Bernie Worrell") was added to the live lineup on keyboards. During the tour, Hynde felt the band's sound had strayed from its [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music") rock roots. She believed that she was now fronting a new band that was "not Pretenders". Partway into the tour, she took drastic action: Stevens and Worrell were both sacked, Malcolm Foster was reinstated on bass, and Rupert Black returned on keyboards.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In mid-1987, McIntosh left the band and was replaced by ex-Smiths guitarist [Johnny Marr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Marr "Johnny Marr"), who remained with the group until early 1988. This iteration of the band, which did not include Cunningham, Foster, or Black, issued one single ("[The Windows of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Windows_of_the_World "The Windows of the World")"/"1969") before dissolving.

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1990s")]

In 1990, Hynde hired session players (including one-time Pretenders Bremner and Cunningham and bassist [John Mckenzie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McKenzie_(musician) "John McKenzie (musician)")) and recorded a new Pretenders album, _[Packed!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packed! "Packed!")_ Hynde was the only person pictured anywhere on the album and was the only official member of the band.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

By 1993, Hynde had teamed with ex-[Katydids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katydids_(band) "Katydids (band)") guitarist [Adam Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Seymour_(musician) "Adam Seymour (musician)") to form a new version of Pretenders. The team of Hynde and Seymour then hired a number of session musicians to record _[Last of the Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last\_of\_the\_Independents "Last of the Independents")_ that year, including ex-Smiths bassist [Andy Rourke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Rourke "Andy Rourke"), ex-[Primitives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Primitives "The Primitives") bassist Andy Hobson, and drummer/writer/producer James Hood, previously with [the Impossible Dreamers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Impossible_Dreamers "The Impossible Dreamers") and [Moodswings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moodswings_(band) "Moodswings (band)"). By the end of the album sessions (and for the subsequent tour), though, the official band line-up was Hynde, Seymour, Hobson, and returning drummer Martin Chambers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

When _Last of the Independents_ was released in 1994, it rated gold in the US. Lead single "Night in my Veins" was a minor success in the US, a mid-chart success in the UK, and a top-10 success in Canada. The second single was the album's centrepiece ballad "[I'll Stand by You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll_Stand_by_You "I'll Stand by You")"; this track received substantial airplay, and was a top-10 success in the UK, and top 20 in the US (number 16 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100) and in Canada.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-The_Great_Rock_Discography-3)

On 10 April 1999, Hynde led the memorial concert "[Here, There, and Everywhere – A Concert for Linda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_for_Linda "Concert for Linda")" for her late close friend [Linda McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McCartney "Linda McCartney") at the [Royal Albert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Albert_Hall "Royal Albert Hall"), London, organised by Hynde and [Carla Lane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carla_Lane "Carla Lane"). Pretenders were the backing band for all artists.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-20)

_[Viva el Amor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viva\_el\_Amor "Viva el Amor")_ was released during 1999, as was their collaboration with [Tom Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Jones_(singer) "Tom Jones (singer)") on the album _[Reload](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reload\_(Tom\_Jones\_album) "Reload (Tom Jones album)")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-22)

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2000s")]

The Pretenders joined with [Emmylou Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmylou_Harris "Emmylou Harris") on _[Return of the Grievous Angel: A Tribute to Gram Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return\_of\_the\_Grievous\_Angel:\_A\_Tribute\_to\_Gram\_Parsons "Return of the Grievous Angel: A Tribute to Gram Parsons")_, performing the song "[She](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She_(Charles_Aznavour_song) "She (Charles Aznavour song)")". A _Greatest Hits_ compilation followed in 2000. During 2002 _[Loose Screw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loose\_Screw "Loose Screw")_ was released by [Artemis Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_Records "Artemis Records"), the first Pretenders record to be released by a company other than WEA. _Rolling Stone_ noted its "refinement, stylish melodies, and vocal fireworks", while _[Blender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blender\_(magazine) "Blender (magazine)")_ called it "slick, snarky pop with flashes of brilliance".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-23)

In March 2005, the Pretenders were inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-25) At the induction ceremony, the band performed "[Precious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precious_(Pretenders_song) "Precious (Pretenders song)")" and "[Message of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message_of_Love "Message of Love")".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-26) During her acceptance speech, Hynde named and thanked all the replacement members of the group, then said:

> "I know that the Pretenders have looked like a tribute band for the last 20 years. ... And we're paying tribute to James Honeyman-Scott and Pete Farndon, without whom we wouldn't be here. And on the other hand, without us, they might have been here, but that's the way it works in rock 'n' roll."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-27)

The Pretenders' album _[Break Up the Concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Break\_Up\_the\_Concrete "Break Up the Concrete")_ was released through [Shangri-La Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shangri-La_Music "Shangri-La Music") on 7 October 2008. It was the band's first top-40 album in the US in 22 years, and its last to date. Tracks include "Boots of Chinese Plastic", "Don't Cut Your Hair", "Love's a Mystery", "The Last Ride", and "Almost Perfect".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-28)

### 2010s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2010s")]

In September 2012, the Pretenders regrouped (Hynde, Chambers, Heywood, Walbourne, and Wilkinson) as part of the entertainment line-up for the [2012 Singapore Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Singapore_Grand_Prix "2012 Singapore Grand Prix").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-29) They were joined by keyboardist/acoustic guitarist [Carwyn Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carwyn_Ellis "Carwyn Ellis") in autumn 2012.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On 6 September 2016, [Stevie Nicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Nicks "Stevie Nicks") announced that the Pretenders would tour with her on a 27-city tour for the last three months of 2016.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-nicks-30) The live band consisted of Hynde, Chambers, Heywood, Walbourne, and Wilkinson, as before.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-31) Pretenders released their 10th studio album, _[Alone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alone\_(Pretenders\_album) "Alone (Pretenders album)")_, on 21 October 2016. However, as on _Packed!_, Hynde was the only Pretender on the album, which was otherwise played entirely by session musicians.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In May 2017, Ellis resumed touring with the Pretenders, who toured [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") with Nicks. In October 2017, the Pretenders appeared on _[Austin City Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin\_City\_Limits "Austin City Limits")_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-32)

### 2020s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Pretenders&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2020s")]

The band was originally scheduled to release their 11th studio album _[Hate for Sale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate\_for\_Sale "Hate for Sale")_ on 1 May 2020, and lead single "The Buzz" was released on 17 March 2020.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-HFS_NME-33) However, on 24 March, the album release was delayed to 17 July.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-34) On the same day (24 March), they released the second single, which is the title track, "Hate for Sale".

On 17 April 2020, their third single, "You Can't Hurt a Fool", was released.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-35) On 12 May 2020, they released their fourth single, "Turf Accountant Daddy".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-36) "Don't Want to be This Lonely", release 28 May 2020, was the fifth and final single from the album.

A five-month North American tour with [Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journey_(band) "Journey (band)") was scheduled to begin on 15 May 2020.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-37) Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the tour was cancelled.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-38)

On 3 September 2022, the Pretenders performed at the [Taylor Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Hawkins "Taylor Hawkins") Tribute Concert at [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium "Wembley Stadium") with [Dave Grohl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Grohl "Dave Grohl") on bass. They performed "Precious", "Tattooed Love Boys", and "Brass in Pocket".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-39)

_[Relentless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relentless\_(The\_Pretenders\_album) "Relentless (The Pretenders album)")_ was announced in May 2023, with a release date of 1 September, which subsequently had been moved to 15 September. The announced line-up for the recording was Chrissie Hynde (vocals), [James Walbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Walbourne "James Walbourne") (guitars), [Carwyn Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carwyn_Ellis "Carwyn Ellis") (keyboards, guitar), Kris Sonne (drums), Chris Hill (double bass), and Nick Wilkinson (bass). The new album announcement coincided with a return to major touring in 2023, starting with various UK, Ireland, and European dates with a wide variety of headline, festival, and support shows reaching the US, Canada, and further European dates to be completed by October.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The group issued a live album, _Kick 'Em Where It Hurts_, in 2025. Around the same time, they toured South America.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders#cite_note-40)

**Sex** (stylised **SEX**) was a [boutique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boutique "Boutique") run by [Vivienne Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood") and her then-partner [Malcolm McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_McLaren "Malcolm McLaren") at 430 [King's Road, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Road,_London "King's Road, London"), between 1974 and 1976. It specialised in clothing that defined the [look of the punk movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_fashion "Punk fashion").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-PM-1)

Westwood and McLaren's boutique underwent several name and correlating interior decor changes through the 1970s to connect with design inspirations, the boutique finally being renamed World's End in 1979, a name which (following a short period of closure) the shop retains to this day.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Pre-_SEX_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-SEX")]

430 Kings Road in London's [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_London "Chelsea, London") district had been the site of several fashion boutiques, including _The 430 Boutique_, operated by Carol Derry and Bill Fuller in the early 1960s; _[Hung On You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hung\_On\_You "Hung On You")_ run by Jane Ormsby Gore and Michael Rainey from 1967 to 1969; [_Mr Freedom_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr_Freedom_(fashion) "Mr Freedom (fashion)") from 1969 to 1970;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-2) and _Paradise Garage_ from 1970 to 1971.

In October 1971, [Malcolm McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_McLaren "Malcolm McLaren") and a friend from art school, Patrick Casey, opened a stall in the back of _Paradise Garage_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-3) selling items collected by McLaren over the previous year, including rock & roll records, magazines, clothing, and memorabilia from the 1950s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:0-4) The following month, Paradise Garage proprietor [Trevor Myles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Myles "Trevor Myles") relinquished the entire premises to McLaren and Casey.

They renamed the shop _Let It Rock_ and stocked it with [second-hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-hand "Second-hand") and new [Teddy Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Boy "Teddy Boy") clothes designed by [Vivienne Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood"), McLaren's then-girlfriend.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:1-5) They painted the shop-front corrugated iron frontage black with the name pasted in pink lettering. The interior was given period detail, such as "Odeon" wallpaper and [Festival of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Britain "Festival of Britain") trinkets, furnished in the style of a 1950s living room.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:0-4) The label was noted for its bespoke tailored drape jackets, skin-tight trousers, and thick-soled "[brothel creepers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brothel_creepers "Brothel creepers")" shoes. _Let It Rock_ was soon covered in the _[London Evening Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London\_Evening\_Standard "London Evening Standard")_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1973, the outlet interior was changed and the shop was renamed _Too Fast To Live, Too Young To Die_, to reflect a new range of clothing from Britain's early 1960s "rocker" fashions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-6) The stock included chains, leather, and sleeveless t-shirts adorned with provocative statements,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:1-5) reflecting Westwood's politically-informed design inspirations. The boutique's name paid homage to [James Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dean "James Dean"). Signage featured a black background with white lettering spelling out the shop's new name around a large [skull and crossbones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skull_and_crossbones "Skull and crossbones"), a new era of [youth subculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_subculture "Youth subculture") was echoed.

### SEX

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: SEX")]

In the spring of 1974, the shop underwent another refurbishment[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:2-7) and was [rebranded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebranding "Rebranding") with the name _SEX_.

The façade[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-marieclaire.co.uk-8) included a 4-foot (1.2 m) sign of pink foam rubber letters spelling "SEX",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-10) and the interior of the boutique was covered with [graffiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graffiti "Graffiti") from the [SCUM Manifesto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCUM_Manifesto "SCUM Manifesto") and chickenwire. Rubber curtains covered the walls and red carpeting was installed.

_SEX_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-11) sold fetish and bondage wear supplied by existing specialist labels such as Atomage, She-And-Me and London Leatherman as well as designs by McLaren and [Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-12)[Pamela Rooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Rooke "Pamela Rooke"), better known as Jordan, was a sales assistant.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-14) Among customers at _SEX_ were the four original members of [Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols") (the bass-player [Glen Matlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Matlock "Glen Matlock") was an employee as a sales assistant on Saturdays). The group's name was provided by McLaren in partial promotion of the boutique. In August 1975, nineteen-year-old [John Lydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lydon "John Lydon") was persuaded to audition for the group by singing along to [Alice Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Cooper "Alice Cooper")'s "[I'm Eighteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Eighteen "I'm Eighteen")" on the jukebox. Other notable patrons included occasional assistant Chrissie Hynde,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-15)[Adam Ant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Ant "Adam Ant"), [Marco Pirroni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pirroni "Marco Pirroni"), [Siouxsie Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siouxsie_Sioux "Siouxsie Sioux"), [Steven Severin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Severin "Steven Severin") and the rest of the [Bromley Contingent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromley_Contingent "Bromley Contingent").

The store's designs confronted social and sexual taboos, and included T-shirts bearing images of the [Cambridge Rapist's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Samuel_Cook "Peter Samuel Cook") face hood,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-16) semi-naked cowboys[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-marieclaire.co.uk-8) from a 1969 illustration by the US artist [Jim French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_French_(photographer) "Jim French (photographer)"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-PG-17) trompe-l'œil bare breasts[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-18) by [Rhode Island School of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_School_of_Design "Rhode Island School of Design") students Janusz and Laura Gottwald in the late 1960s,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-PG-17) and pornographic texts from the book _School for Wives_ ("I groaned with pain...in a soft corrosion")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-21) by the beat author [Alexander Trocchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Trocchi "Alexander Trocchi"). Also featured were T-shirts[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-22) with the slogan 'Prick Up Your Ears',[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-23) a reference to the biography of influential proto-punk subversive [Joe Orton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Orton "Joe Orton"), and text culled from the biography of Orton stating how cheap clothes suited him. Among the designs were clear plastic-pocketed jeans, zippered tops and the _Anarchy shirt_[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-25) which used dead stock from the 1960s manufacturer Wemblex.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-27) These were bleached and dyed shirts and adorned with silk [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx") patches and anarchist slogans.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-32)

### Seditionaries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Seditionaries")]

In December 1976, 430 King's Road was renamed _Seditionaries_,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-34) trading under that title until September 1980.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-35) As _Seditionaries: Clothes for Heroes_, the boutique adopted brutalist interior and exterior styling: large murals depicting imagery of bomb damage, harshly bright lighting, and cavities perforating the ceiling created by McLaren,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:2-7) surrounded [Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood")'s innovative garments now considered punk signatures.

Designs were licensed by Westwood to the operators of the boutique at 153 King's Road, **Boy** (formerly _[Acme Attractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acme\_Attractions "Acme Attractions")_)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-36) who issued them, some with alterations, over the next eight years.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-37)**Boy** London was founded by Stephane Raynor[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-38) and Israel-based businessman John Krivine[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-39) in 1976 on the King's Road.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-41) Krivine sold the company in 1984.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-independent.co.uk-42)

### World's End

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: World's End")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Athitaya_Restaurant%2C_430_King%27s_Road%2C_London_SW10_0LJ%2C_4_June_2011.jpg/250px-Athitaya_Restaurant%2C_430_King%27s_Road%2C_London_SW10_0LJ%2C_4_June_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Athitaya_Restaurant,_430_King's_Road,_London_SW10_0LJ,_4_June_2011.jpg)

World's End

In late 1980, the shop at 430 King's Road re-opened under the name _World's End_. The building was designed by McLaren and Westwood and realised by [Roger Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_K._Burton "Roger K. Burton"), aided by Jeremy Blackburn and Tony Devers, to resemble a mixture of the Olde Curiosity Shoppe and an 18th-century galleon. The façade was installed with a large clock which spun backwards with the floor raked at an angle. McLaren and Westwood launched the first of a series of collections[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-43) from the outlet at the beginning of 1981 and collaborated for a further three years. _World's End_ remains open as part of Vivienne Westwood's global fashion empire.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-44)

**Sex** (stylised **SEX**) was a [boutique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boutique "Boutique") run by [Vivienne Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood") and her then-partner [Malcolm McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_McLaren "Malcolm McLaren") at 430 [King's Road, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Road,_London "King's Road, London"), between 1974 and 1976. It specialised in clothing that defined the [look of the punk movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_fashion "Punk fashion").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-PM-1)

Westwood and McLaren's boutique underwent several name and correlating interior decor changes through the 1970s to connect with design inspirations, the boutique finally being renamed World's End in 1979, a name which (following a short period of closure) the shop retains to this day.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Pre-_SEX_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-SEX")]

430 Kings Road in London's [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea,_London "Chelsea, London") district had been the site of several fashion boutiques, including _The 430 Boutique_, operated by Carol Derry and Bill Fuller in the early 1960s; _[Hung On You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hung\_On\_You "Hung On You")_ run by Jane Ormsby Gore and Michael Rainey from 1967 to 1969; [_Mr Freedom_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr_Freedom_(fashion) "Mr Freedom (fashion)") from 1969 to 1970;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-2) and _Paradise Garage_ from 1970 to 1971.

In October 1971, [Malcolm McLaren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_McLaren "Malcolm McLaren") and a friend from art school, Patrick Casey, opened a stall in the back of _Paradise Garage_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-3) selling items collected by McLaren over the previous year, including rock & roll records, magazines, clothing, and memorabilia from the 1950s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:0-4) The following month, Paradise Garage proprietor [Trevor Myles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Myles "Trevor Myles") relinquished the entire premises to McLaren and Casey.

They renamed the shop _Let It Rock_ and stocked it with [second-hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-hand "Second-hand") and new [Teddy Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Boy "Teddy Boy") clothes designed by [Vivienne Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood"), McLaren's then-girlfriend.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:1-5) They painted the shop-front corrugated iron frontage black with the name pasted in pink lettering. The interior was given period detail, such as "Odeon" wallpaper and [Festival of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Britain "Festival of Britain") trinkets, furnished in the style of a 1950s living room.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:0-4) The label was noted for its bespoke tailored drape jackets, skin-tight trousers, and thick-soled "[brothel creepers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brothel_creepers "Brothel creepers")" shoes. _Let It Rock_ was soon covered in the _[London Evening Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London\_Evening\_Standard "London Evening Standard")_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1973, the outlet interior was changed and the shop was renamed _Too Fast To Live, Too Young To Die_, to reflect a new range of clothing from Britain's early 1960s "rocker" fashions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-6) The stock included chains, leather, and sleeveless t-shirts adorned with provocative statements,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:1-5) reflecting Westwood's politically-informed design inspirations. The boutique's name paid homage to [James Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dean "James Dean"). Signage featured a black background with white lettering spelling out the shop's new name around a large [skull and crossbones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skull_and_crossbones "Skull and crossbones"), a new era of [youth subculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_subculture "Youth subculture") was echoed.

### SEX

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: SEX")]

In the spring of 1974, the shop underwent another refurbishment[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:2-7) and was [rebranded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebranding "Rebranding") with the name _SEX_.

The façade[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-marieclaire.co.uk-8) included a 4-foot (1.2 m) sign of pink foam rubber letters spelling "SEX",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-10) and the interior of the boutique was covered with [graffiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graffiti "Graffiti") from the [SCUM Manifesto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCUM_Manifesto "SCUM Manifesto") and chickenwire. Rubber curtains covered the walls and red carpeting was installed.

_SEX_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-11) sold fetish and bondage wear supplied by existing specialist labels such as Atomage, She-And-Me and London Leatherman as well as designs by McLaren and [Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-12)[Pamela Rooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Rooke "Pamela Rooke"), better known as Jordan, was a sales assistant.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-14) Among customers at _SEX_ were the four original members of [Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols") (the bass-player [Glen Matlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Matlock "Glen Matlock") was an employee as a sales assistant on Saturdays). The group's name was provided by McLaren in partial promotion of the boutique. In August 1975, nineteen-year-old [John Lydon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lydon "John Lydon") was persuaded to audition for the group by singing along to [Alice Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Cooper "Alice Cooper")'s "[I'm Eighteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'm_Eighteen "I'm Eighteen")" on the jukebox. Other notable patrons included occasional assistant Chrissie Hynde,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-15)[Adam Ant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Ant "Adam Ant"), [Marco Pirroni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pirroni "Marco Pirroni"), [Siouxsie Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siouxsie_Sioux "Siouxsie Sioux"), [Steven Severin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Severin "Steven Severin") and the rest of the [Bromley Contingent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromley_Contingent "Bromley Contingent").

The store's designs confronted social and sexual taboos, and included T-shirts bearing images of the [Cambridge Rapist's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Samuel_Cook "Peter Samuel Cook") face hood,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-16) semi-naked cowboys[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-marieclaire.co.uk-8) from a 1969 illustration by the US artist [Jim French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_French_(photographer) "Jim French (photographer)"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-PG-17) trompe-l'œil bare breasts[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-18) by [Rhode Island School of Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island_School_of_Design "Rhode Island School of Design") students Janusz and Laura Gottwald in the late 1960s,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-PG-17) and pornographic texts from the book _School for Wives_ ("I groaned with pain...in a soft corrosion")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-21) by the beat author [Alexander Trocchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Trocchi "Alexander Trocchi"). Also featured were T-shirts[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-22) with the slogan 'Prick Up Your Ears',[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-23) a reference to the biography of influential proto-punk subversive [Joe Orton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Orton "Joe Orton"), and text culled from the biography of Orton stating how cheap clothes suited him. Among the designs were clear plastic-pocketed jeans, zippered tops and the _Anarchy shirt_[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-25) which used dead stock from the 1960s manufacturer Wemblex.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-27) These were bleached and dyed shirts and adorned with silk [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx") patches and anarchist slogans.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-32)

### Seditionaries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Seditionaries")]

In December 1976, 430 King's Road was renamed _Seditionaries_,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-34) trading under that title until September 1980.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-35) As _Seditionaries: Clothes for Heroes_, the boutique adopted brutalist interior and exterior styling: large murals depicting imagery of bomb damage, harshly bright lighting, and cavities perforating the ceiling created by McLaren,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-:2-7) surrounded [Westwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Westwood "Vivienne Westwood")'s innovative garments now considered punk signatures.

Designs were licensed by Westwood to the operators of the boutique at 153 King's Road, **Boy** (formerly _[Acme Attractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acme\_Attractions "Acme Attractions")_)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-36) who issued them, some with alterations, over the next eight years.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-37)**Boy** London was founded by Stephane Raynor[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-38) and Israel-based businessman John Krivine[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-39) in 1976 on the King's Road.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-41) Krivine sold the company in 1984.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-independent.co.uk-42)

### World's End

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sex_(boutique)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: World's End")]

World's End

In late 1980, the shop at 430 King's Road re-opened under the name _World's End_. The building was designed by McLaren and Westwood and realised by [Roger Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_K._Burton "Roger K. Burton"), aided by Jeremy Blackburn and Tony Devers, to resemble a mixture of the Olde Curiosity Shoppe and an 18th-century galleon. The façade was installed with a large clock which spun backwards with the floor raked at an angle. McLaren and Westwood launched the first of a series of collections[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-43) from the outlet at the beginning of 1981 and collaborated for a further three years. _World's End_ remains open as part of Vivienne Westwood's global fashion empire.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_(boutique)#cite_note-44)
